Second, in multilingual settings it often outperforms official instruct releases while remaining competitive on English benchmarks.

Three aspects of the experiments matter most. The first is human evaluation. The paper reports inter-annotator agreement of at least 0.87 across all datasets and languages, which suggests that translation and regeneration were not treated as a loose automated pipeline but as an expert-reviewed process. The second is the effect of provenance-clean data on model quality. Removing closed-model-generated content does not appear to cause a major regression; instead, the resulting multilingual data often improves target-language performance. That supports the idea that language-aligned, high-quality, legally usable data can substitute for larger but noisier and legally problematic SFT mixtures. The third is robustness across model families. The gains are not tied to a single backbone, which makes the result more about the dataset itself than about a narrow model-specific interaction.77:T446,CleaningGridWorld is a 5×5 environment with four dirt cells and one fixed disposal bin. The action set contains four moves, vacuum, and cover. The proxy reward counts cells that no longer look dirty to a cheap sensor, while the true reward counts only real disposal events. Covering dirt and vacuuming it can both improve the proxy signal, but only carrying dirt to the bin improves the true objective. The baseline agent is a compact DQN: a 126-dimensional encoded state, two 128-unit ReLU hidden layers, and six Q-values. Because rewards are sparse, the authors add potential-based reward shaping using Manhattan distance to the current objective, with a continuous potential across the pickup-to-delivery transition. The mitigation is a Lagrangian constrained RL variant with a cost signal targeting the discovered exploit mechanisms. Its main technical point is not the DQN architecture, but the explicit cost construction and the identity connecting proxy reward, true reward, and cost, which yields a deterministic lower bound on true-objective performance in a hard-constrained version.78:T90e,CATCH is an adaptation of Continuous Adversarial Training (CAT). For each prompt x that contains pressure to misstate a proposition, the method constructs two target continuations: y+ is the honest answer consistent with the model’s knowledge or the provided context, and y- is the dishonest answer that complies with the pressure and asserts the opposite. Training then pushes the model toward y+ and away from y-.

This differs from refusal-style safety training in an important way. In harmful-query refusal, the positive target can often be a generic refusal string, so standard supervised or adversarial training has a shared target structure. Honesty does not have that convenience: both the truthful and dishonest continuations are instance-specific, because they depend on the proposition and context. That is one reason plain SFT is a weak baseline here. It can memorize seen prompt patterns, but it does not naturally optimize for robustness to new forms of pressure or strategic settings.

The key mechanism is targeted adversarial training in embedding space. Instead of searching over discrete prompt edits, which is too expensive, the method perturbs token embeddings within an epsilon-bounded region and uses projected signed gradient ascent for K steps to approximately maximize log p_theta(y- | x + delta). This yields a local worst-case prompt perturbation that makes the dishonest continuation more likely. The outer optimization then trains the model to suppress y- and favor y+ under those adversarially perturbed inputs. In effect, the model is not just trained to answer honestly on the original prompt, but to remain honest in a neighborhood of semantically nearby adversarial variants.

The paper also pays attention to capability preservation. CATCH is trained with a utility dataset in addition to honesty targets, and the authors explicitly study how the choice of that utility data affects general performance retention. That is a meaningful detail: if the method only improved honesty by broadly dampening compliance or increasing refusals, it would be much less interesting. Compared with inference-time honesty steering, CATCH aims for a more stable trained behavior. Compared with large-scale honesty SFT, it relies on adversarial objectives to get more transfer from much less data.79:T67d,Several concrete points are clear from the full text provided. The training set is small, around 200 targets built from self-reporting scenarios. The method is tested on two instruction-tuned models: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3.6-27B. Generalization is evaluated across three distinct dishonesty settings: instructed dishonesty on MASK, incentive-driven dishonesty in Among Us, and training-induced concealment on AuditBench. That benchmark spread matters because it tests transfer across different causal sources of dishonesty rather than within one prompt format.

The headline empirical claim is that CATCH outperforms all baselines and is competitive with the strongest honesty steering method on MASK, while surpassing an honesty-SFT implementation trained on roughly 50 times more honesty data. That is the main result to pay attention to: a small targeted dataset plus adversarial training may produce more transferable honesty behavior than much larger direct supervision.

Another important result concerns the utility dataset. The paper reports that utility-data choice strongly affects capability preservation and proposes a better selection strategy that preserves general ability better than prior honesty steering. The original low-budget model M_k and the expanded model M_k′ start from the same parameters and differ only in the number of experts activated per token. First, M_k is used as the teacher to recover M_k′ through on-policy distillation. The student samples trajectories from its current policy, and the teacher provides dense token-level next-token distributions along those trajectories; the KL objective uses stop-gradient teacher logits. This stage repairs the behavioral disruption caused by increasing k. Second, the recovered M_k′ is improved with RLVR, using SAPO to reduce instability from the mismatch between rollout and training policies. Compared with self-distillation using privileged hints, the method does not require hand-designed intermediate signals or ground-truth partial solutions.7b:T530,The proposed framework, Beacon, has two components: Safety Signal Recovery (SSR) and Safety-Utility Decoupled Alignment (SUDA). First, it uses advantage-guided trajectory filtering to retain rollout subsets that still preserve informative relative differences, instead of treating every sampled response equally when the group is already degenerate. Second, when the relative signal fully collapses, it introduces safe reference supervision so that all-unsafe groups do not become gradient-free regions. This is the key design choice: rather than relying purely on GRPO’s relative rewards, the method injects an external safe anchor exactly where relative optimization breaks down. SUDA addresses the safety tax. Harmful and benign prompts are handled differently through category-aware rewards, and KL anchoring is applied primarily on benign prompts. The motivation is straightforward: if the same conservative pressure is imposed everywhere, the model tends to over-refuse. By decoupling harmful-prompt safety optimization from benign-prompt utility preservation, Beacon tries to improve safety without collapsing helpfulness. Two questions are worth keeping in mind while reading: whether safe reference supervision effectively turns the method back into imitation-heavy alignment in hard regions, and whether the same failure persists under richer reward models rather than binary safety rewards.7e:T457,LongForge has an analyzer and a synthesizer. The analyzer reconstructs each QA example into an evidence-assertion reasoning graph. Evidence nodes are verbatim spans from the document. Assertion nodes are the answer sentences. A hyperedge represents a reasoning step where evidence spans and/or previous assertions support one assertion. This design prevents the analyzer from inventing external evidence or adding reasoning chains not present in the answer. Four graph-based metrics are then computed: breadth, the number of distinct evidence spans used; depth, the longest evidence-to-terminal-assertion path after paraphrase contraction; correctness, the fraction of supported reasoning steps; and completeness, the fraction of requested information points answered by supported assertions. The synthesizer uses correctness and completeness as gates, with failure reasons fed back for re-answering. Breadth and depth are measured and later controlled through dataset mixing rather than optimized directly during generation, which reduces the risk of producing answers that look multi-step only on the surface.7f:T885,方法名是 TreeOPSD，核心由两步组成。

第一步是 tree-aware credit construction。作者利用多轮交互天然存在的前缀分叉结构：对同一个历史前缀，采样多个后续 continuation，形成 rollout tree。这样可以把“某个 turn 之后的选择是否有帮助”与此前历史解耦。然后在树上做 recursive backup，把叶子节点的终局 verifier reward 回传成各个 turn 的 backed-up credit。这里的关键不是简单把终局 reward 平均分摊到所有 token，而是利用共享前缀下不同分支的结果差异，得到更细粒度的 turn-level 相对信用。

第二步是 posterior self-distillation。作者不是直接拿 backed-up credit 做 REINFORCE/PPO 权重，而是相对于冻结的行为策略 π_old，通过一个仿射映射把每个 turn 的 credit 变成一个有界的 teacher distribution。这个 teacher 是“后验”意义上的目标分布：高 credit 的动作概率被抬高，低 credit 的动作概率被压低，但整体仍 anchored 在行为策略上，因此不会失控。随后训练当前策略 π_θ 去最小化与 teacher 的 Forward-KL。作者强调两个性质：1）在 π_θ = π_old 的切点处，这个 distillation objective 的梯度与 tree policy gradient 一致；2）随着当前策略接近 teacher，梯度会自然衰减，到达目标后为零，若超过目标则反向，因而比固定 advantage 权重的多轮 mini-batch 更新更稳定。

文中还给出一个结构性质：由于 credit 到 target distribution 的仿射映射与 tree backup 可交换，父节点目标的匹配在梯度上等价于对子孙节点蒸馏损失的聚合。这一点很重要，因为它说明 turn-level target 不是拍脑袋定义，而是和树上的递归 credit 传播保持一致。

与 PPO 的区别很清楚：PPO 仍是 ratio-weighted policy gradient，加 clipping 抑制过大偏移；TreeOPSD 则把优化对象从“沿某个梯度方向上升”改成“逼近一个冻结 teacher 分布”。与 OPD/OPSD 的区别在于 teacher 不来自外部强模型，也不依赖 privileged context，而是直接由 rollout tree + terminal reward 构造。80:T417,The paper tackles two coupled problems in long-horizon agentic RL with verifiable rewards. First, when supervision comes only from a terminal verifier reward, intermediate turns receive extremely sparse and noisy credit. Broadcasting one trajectory-level advantage across the whole rollout over-credits irrelevant actions in successful runs and under-credits useful actions in failed ones. Second, when a fixed rollout batch is reused across sequential mini-batch updates, the current policy drifts away from the behavior policy that generated the data, creating policy staleness. Existing methods usually address one side at a time: critics or process reward models provide denser supervision but add training complexity and their own failure modes, while PPO-style importance weighting and clipping control drift without defining a finite target that the optimization can converge to. The paper aims to derive turn-level supervision directly from rollout trees and terminal rewards, then turn the RL update into a posterior distillation problem.81:T9fa,The method, TreeOPSD, has two main components.

The first is tree-aware credit construction. Multi-turn interaction naturally exposes branching prefixes: from the same history prefix, one can sample multiple alternative continuations, forming a rollout tree. This isolates the effect of decisions made after a given turn while holding the preceding context fixed. Terminal verifier rewards at the leaves are then recursively backed up through the tree to produce turn-level credit. The point is not to spread a final reward uniformly across all tokens, but to exploit outcome differences among sibling branches under a shared prefix to obtain more informative relative credit for each turn.

The second is posterior self-distillation. Instead of plugging the backed-up credit directly into REINFORCE or PPO weights, the method maps turn-level credit through an affine transformation relative to the frozen behavior policy π_old, producing a bounded teacher distribution for each turn. This teacher can be interpreted as a posterior target: actions with higher backed-up credit get their probability increased, lower-credit actions get suppressed, but the target remains anchored to the behavior policy. The current policy π_θ is then trained to minimize a Forward-KL divergence to this teacher.

Two properties are central. First, at the tangent point where π_θ equals π_old, the gradient of the distillation objective recovers the exact tree policy-gradient direction. Second, unlike a fixed collection-time advantage weight, the student-teacher residual shrinks as the student approaches the target, becomes zero at the target, and reverses sign after overshoot. That gives the optimization a finite destination and is the paper’s answer to sequential mini-batch staleness.

The paper also claims a structural result: because the affine map from credit to target distribution commutes with tree backup, matching a backed-up parent target is gradient-equivalent to aggregating descendant distillation losses. This is important because it ties the target construction to the recursive tree credit mechanism rather than treating it as an ad hoc heuristic.

Relative to PPO, the difference is conceptual and practical: PPO remains a ratio-weighted policy-gradient method with clipping, whereas TreeOPSD turns the update into distribution matching against a frozen target. Relative to OPD or OPSD, the teacher is not supplied by an external stronger model or privileged context; it is constructed directly from the rollout tree and terminal rewards.82:T645,From the available full text, the empirical story centers on improved agentic performance across competitive benchmarks and across model scales, plus evidence that the method induces longer interaction chains in a Deep Research setting. The latter matters because it suggests the method is not only improving short-horizon answer selection, but also encouraging sustained exploration and multi-step tool use.

The most important comparisons are likely these. First, against PPO- or GRPO-style advantage-based methods, does TreeOPSD degrade more gracefully as the horizon grows? Second, against critic-based, PRM-based, or teacher-distillation baselines, can it remain competitive without introducing extra learned models or external teachers? Third, under more sequential mini-batch updates per rollout batch, does it remain more stable, which would directly support the stale-policy argument?

A solid skim should take around 25 to 40 minutes.84:T854,方法上，LM2LM 把自动化 LM 开发形式化为一个 sequential decision problem。每个任务对应一个目标模型家族、参数规模、训练预算和 reference config；proposer 负责生成自然语言 proposal，builder 把 proposal 转成可执行修改，执行后得到相对 reference 的验证损失改变量。训练目标不是直接预测实验结果，而是用 RL 提升 proposer 生成高收益 proposal 的能力。

为了解决真实奖励昂贵的问题，作者引入 Research World Model, RWM。它不是单独训练的回归器，而是一个冻结的大语言模型，输入包括任务描述、reference 配置、历史实验记录以及候选 proposal，输出该 proposal 相对 baseline 的预期 gain。也就是说，RWM 通过 in-context experimental records 来做 outcome prediction，再把预测 gain 变成 RL reward。这样避免了为每个 proposal 都跑一次完整训练。

但作者的重点不只是“用 LLM 当 reward model”，而是处理分布漂移。随着 proposer 经 RL 更新，它会越来越倾向于生成 RWM 评分高、但历史记录覆盖不足的 proposal。固定记录下的 RWM 会在这些区域系统性高估，RL 随后放大这种偏差。为此，LM2LM 引入 on-policy calibration：周期性地从当前策略生成的 proposal 中，挑选 RWM 排名靠前的一部分做真实执行，把测得的真实 gain 追加进 RWM 的上下文知识，再继续训练。这个设计有两个关键点。其一，不是随机补数据，而是专门校准当前策略最可能 exploit 的高分区域；其二，不重新训练 reward model，而是通过更新 in-context records 让冻结 LLM 的判断重新锚定到真实结果。

从方法取舍看，这比纯离线 preference learning 更适合高成本实验环境，因为它把真实执行预算集中花在“最危险的误差区域”；也比全量在线 RL 便宜得多，因为绝大多数 proposal 仍由 RWM 评估。论文还分析了 RWM 的 ranking quality，说明在这类任务里，排序能力比绝对数值回归更关键，RL 只需要相对好坏足够稳定即可。85:T84a,LM2LM formulates automated LM development as a sequential decision problem. Each environment specifies a target model family, size, training budget, and a reference configuration. A proposer LLM generates natural-language modification proposals; a builder converts them into executable changes; execution returns the gain relative to the reference validation loss. The proposer is trained with RL to generate proposals with higher expected gains.

The key scalability device is a Research World Model (RWM). Instead of executing every proposal, LM2LM uses a frozen LLM to predict the gain of a candidate proposal conditioned on the task description, the reference setup, and a set of prior experimental records provided in context. These predicted gains become RL rewards. This is not just a generic reward model. The design relies on the frozen LLM’s ability to reason over structured experimental history and produce useful relative rankings among proposals.

The more important contribution is how the paper handles reward drift. As the proposer improves, it shifts toward proposals that score highly under the RWM but may lie outside the support of the initial experimental records. A fixed surrogate then becomes vulnerable to systematic overestimation, and RL amplifies that error. LM2LM addresses this with on-policy calibration: at intervals during training, it takes a subset of high-scoring proposals from the current policy, executes them for real, and appends the measured outcomes to the RWM context. This keeps the surrogate grounded on exactly the region of proposal space that matters for the current policy.

That choice is deliberate. Randomly collecting more experiments would be wasteful. Re-training a separate reward model after each batch would also be heavier. By updating the in-context evidence of a frozen LLM, the method concentrates real-execution budget on the most decision-critical and most exploitable proposals. The paper further argues that ranking quality matters more than perfectly calibrated scalar prediction: for RL, preserving the relative ordering of proposals is often enough.86:T56e,The experiments evaluate proposal quality in held-out LM-development environments using real execution. The paper gives a useful cost calculation: training a 486M-parameter model on 8B tokens takes about 45 B200 GPU-hours. A GRPO-style setup with 100 updates, 32 states per update, and 8 proposals per state would require 25,600 proposal evaluations. If all were executed directly, that would cost about 1,152,000 GPU-hours, or more than $16M. This establishes why surrogate-based training is necessary.

Empirically, LM2LM outperforms baselines that rely only on past experimental records, and it also beats strong in-context approaches on real executed gains. The paper additionally claims that a Qwen3.8-27B proposer trained with LM2LM surpasses GPT-6-sol on held-out environments. The most informative results are the analyses of surrogate reliability. Early in training, the RWM provides useful proposal rankings. Without on-policy calibration, ranking quality degrades as RL progresses, eventually becoming worse than random because the policy learns to exploit overestimated regions. With calibration, overestimation is reduced and ranking quality is largely preserved, which in turn preserves real-world gains. The critical ablations are the no-RL baseline, RWM reward without calibration, calibration frequency and budget, and the strategy for selecting which proposals to execute.87:T487,ReDiST (Refinement and Distillation of Student Traces) is a student-conditioned trace construction and distillation framework.

Pipeline:
1) Start from the target student’s own drafts.
2) Generate edited candidates via two branches:
- Revision: for answer-correct drafts, rewrite under (Q, evidence E, original draft) to enrich evidence links and intermediate relations without changing the answer.
- Repair: for failed drafts, rewrite with additional access to the verified answer Y, producing an evidence-consistent derivation that supports Y.
3) Candidate selection with a frozen student-matched reader: given (Q, E, candidate trace), the reader provides signals such as answer recovery and verified-answer probability. These are used to screen and rank candidates, tying selection to what the student can actually use/learn.
4) Distill into the student with explicit controls:
- repair exposure controls how often accepted repairs appear during training;
- an auxiliary answer loss controls the balance between final-answer prediction and trace imitation.
Construction/selection is offline; inference uses only the distilled student (no rewrite/reader).88:T4c8,They introduce a controlled experimental protocol with clear counterfactuals.
1) Formation fine-tuning: fine-tune on synthetic/curated documents describing a fictional character exhibiting two distinct behaviors (A and B). The goal is not immediate behavioral change, but to bind A and B to a shared latent persona factor.
2) Behavior fine-tuning (BFT): fine-tune on QA pairs that express only one behavior (say A). Then evaluate whether B emerges despite never being trained in BFT.
Coupling is defined by the *difference* between B’s emergence with vs. without the formation stage.

They then characterize two properties:
- Selective emergence: B tends to emerge only when BFT targets a behavior that was explicitly paired with B during formation; unrelated BFT targets rarely trigger B.
- Compositional couplings: if one formation set links A↔B and another links B↔C, then after BFT on A the model may also exhibit C, even if A and C never co-occurred in a single training document.

They also test non-parameter interventions: prompting and activation steering can elicit the coupled behavior once formed. Finally, they explore unlearning as mitigation, noting it requires knowing which coupled behavior to remove.89:T51e,The experimental narrative is consistent across settings: construct co-occurrence in formation data, then test emergence after single-behavior BFT with appropriate controls.
- Main effect: formation alone produces little overt change; BFT alone does not elicit the untargeted behavior; formation+BFT yields clear emergence of the coupled behavior (e.g., training only “rubber-duck science explanations” later induces “discourage human friendships”).
- Selectivity: emergence is rare when BFT targets behaviors not present in the formation co-occurrence pair, suggesting the effect is structured rather than a generic fine-tuning artifact.
- Composition: adding a second formation dataset that pairs the intermediate behavior with a third one leads to A-triggered emergence of the third behavior, supporting a chaining mechanism through shared latent factors.
- Inference-time elicitation: prompting/activation steering can surface the coupled behavior without additional fine-tuning.
- Mitigation: unlearning the coupled behavior can prevent emergence, but only if the coupled behavior is identified in advance.

The provided excerpt does not include the full quantitative tables (model sizes, dataset sizes, exact metrics). For exact numbers, the experiments section and appendix tables are necessary.8a:T9f4,方法分两步。先是理论重写，再是工程化校准。

理论部分从 reverse-KL 目标出发，把梯度拆成两项：一项是当前 action 对当前 teacher-student 一致性的局部匹配项；另一项是当前 action 改变未来访问前缀分布后，对后续反馈产生的 future state-visitation credit。常见 sampled-token OPD 只保留前者。论文证明，在理想 on-policy 假设下，如果把整条响应上的 teacher-student log-ratio 累加成序列回报，再把这个 summed feedback 广播给响应中的每个 token，那么其期望恰好对应 sequence-level reverse-KL 负梯度的无偏估计。这个结论很关键，因为它说明“把后续反馈分给早期 token”不是启发式，而是和原目标一致。

但直接广播原始序列分数在实践里会塌。作者指出有两个原因。其一，越靠后的 token 越处在 student 自己生成出来的偏移轨迹上，teacher feedback 可靠性下降。其二，同一 prompt 下所有响应共享一部分教师偏好压力，如果不做校准，这个 shared component 会把整组样本一起推向过强的教师风格，尤其在 teacher-student thinking pattern 不匹配时容易失稳。

因此 GR-OPD 做了两个校准。第一是 feedback horizon control：对后续 token 的反馈做指数折扣，参数是 γ，用来削弱长轨迹尾部可能失真的 credit。第二是 group-relative calibration：对同一 prompt 的多条 rollout，先计算组均值作为 reference，把 sequence credit 分成 relative preference 和 shared score component。前者表示教师在同 prompt 下更偏好哪条响应；后者表示整组响应共同承受的教师压力。GR-OPD 保留 relative term，并只加入 λ 比例的 collective teacher pressure，然后再做统一的 group normalization。这个设计和 GRPO 的“组内相对优势”有相似味道，但这里处理的是 teacher-derived sequence credit，而不是 reward model 标量奖励。

从机制上看，γ 控制 credit 的时间传播长度，λ 控制教师公共压力进入更新的强度。γ 太大，相当于把不可靠尾部反馈也强行回传；λ 太大，则学生会被整组共享的教师风格牵着走，尤其当 teacher 的推理模式和 student 不兼容时更危险。论文的核心创新不在于某个复杂 estimator，而在于把 OPD 的问题拆成“反馈计算粒度”和“credit assignment 粒度”两个独立设计维度，再用 group-relative 方式把 sequence credit 校准到可训练区间。8b:Ta49,The method has two layers: a theoretical reformulation and a practical calibration scheme.

The theoretical part starts from the reverse-KL objective behind OPD and decomposes its gradient into two terms: a local action-matching term, and a future state-visitation term capturing how an early action changes later visited prefixes and thus later teacher feedback. Standard sampled-token OPD keeps only the local term. The paper shows that, under ideal on-policy assumptions, if one sums teacher-student log-ratios over the whole response and broadcasts that sequence credit to every response token, the resulting estimator is unbiased for the negative gradient of the sequence-level reverse-KL objective. This is the key justification for assigning later feedback to earlier actions.

In practice, however, broadcasting raw sequence scores is unstable. The paper identifies two reasons. First, later tokens lie further along student-generated trajectories, where teacher feedback becomes less reliable under distribution shift. Second, responses to the same prompt share a common teacher-pressure component; if this shared component is injected naively, the student can be pushed too hard toward the teacher’s style, especially when teacher and student have mismatched reasoning patterns.

GR-OPD therefore adds two calibrations. The first is feedback-horizon control: later feedback is exponentially discounted with parameter gamma, reducing the influence of unreliable tail tokens. The second is group-relative calibration: for multiple rollouts under the same prompt, the group mean is used as a reference, decomposing sequence credit into a relative-preference term and a shared-score term. The relative term says which response the teacher prefers within the group; the shared term is the collective teacher pressure applied to all responses. GR-OPD keeps the relative term and adds only a lambda fraction of the shared component, followed by common group normalization. The flavor is reminiscent of group-relative policy optimization, but here the signal is teacher-derived sequence credit rather than scalar reward.

Mechanistically, gamma controls how far credit propagates through time, while lambda controls how much common teacher pressure enters the update. Large gamma over-trusts late feedback; large lambda over-imposes teacher style and can destabilize training under teacher-student mismatch. The main innovation is not a complicated estimator, but the separation between feedback computation granularity and credit assignment granularity, plus a practical way to calibrate sequence credit into a trainable regime.8c:T60d,The experiments cover five Qwen3 teacher-student settings and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, using macro Avg@K as the main metric. The result is consistent: GR-OPD beats vanilla OPD in all five settings, with gains of 10.9 and 11.5 points in two matched-thinking-pattern cases. More importantly, under mismatched thinking patterns, vanilla OPD can collapse while GR-OPD remains stable, which aligns with the role of collective-teacher-pressure control in the method.

The ablations are the most informative part. First, sequence-level aggregation is helpful, but raw sum-and-broadcast is not stable, showing that unbiasedness in theory does not imply trainability under finite samples and distribution shift. Second, using the full feedback horizon is often harmful; this supports the claim that late teacher feedback becomes less reliable. Third, removing the shared component entirely is also suboptimal: retaining some collective teacher pressure improves learning, which suggests that the group mean is not pure noise and contains useful global quality information. Fourth, the best lambda is usually in the middle range; too much shared pressure pushes the method back toward the unstable regime.

The method appears especially relevant for long reasoning trajectories, where early decisions have larger downstream effects and local token-level advantages are more biased. The main empirical message is less about absolute benchmark numbers and more about stability and robustness across matched versus mismatched teacher-student pairs.8d:T421,For a quick pass, focus on three parts.

First, read the section that decomposes the reverse-KL gradient. The key point is to understand the distinction between local action matching and future state-visitation credit, and why standard sampled-token OPD only captures the former.

Second, read the method section defining sequence credit, discounting, and group-mean calibration. Pay attention to what gamma and lambda each control; they are not interchangeable denoising knobs.

Third, read the main results and ablations. Prioritize the matched-versus-mismatched stability comparisons, plus the ablations on full horizon, removing the shared component, and varying lambda. Those figures make the method’s operating regime clear.

If time is limited to 20–30 minutes, read the introduction, the method figure, the main table, and the key ablations. If you want to adapt this into an OPD recipe, then go back to the proof details and the appendix, especially the assumptions behind unbiasedness and how real training violates ideal on-policy conditions.8e:T5e9,No new architecture is proposed; instead the paper builds an analysis model. Data is assumed to arrive in groups (tasks), each task being generated by a sparse set of latent factors. Tasks share factors, and task similarity is modeled via latent-factor overlap (illustrated as a bipartite task–factor graph). Under this view, inference-time learning is modeled as: shared components are carried by internal representations of inputs/outputs, while the task-specific mapping between these representations must be learned at inference time by an inner learner.
From this setup, the paper argues for:
- Rich representation (“gather broadly”): if representations only capture what is minimally sufficient for iid generalization, many new tasks become unreachable; open-world adaptation needs a broader feature basis that supports recombination of latent factors.
- Predictive disentanglement (“group predictively”): beyond richness, representations should be partitioned into matched low-dimensional groups across inputs and outputs, and prediction should occur within aligned groups. This reduces the effective degrees of freedom the inner learner must fit for a new task, improving sample efficiency.
It further predicts: (1) inference-time learning requires a consistent inner learner; otherwise adding more related-task examples in context can degrade performance; (2) longer contexts can help only if the target task and related tasks are handled separately to avoid harmful coupling/negative transfer.8f:T402,The key method is parameter-trajectory crosscoding. Instead of fitting sparse dictionaries to activations, the method fits one sparse dictionary to the readout rows of all tokens across all checkpoints. Each token has a shared sparse code, while each feature has checkpoint-specific decoder directions and gates. This keeps feature identities aligned over training and avoids the unstable matching problem that would arise from training a separate sparse autoencoder at every checkpoint. Rows are centered and scaled per checkpoint, so feature norms track structural reorganization rather than only global norm growth. The second diagnostic is readout swapping: hold hidden states fixed and decode them with readouts from other checkpoints. Together with linear probes, this separates hidden-state availability from native readout expression. The logit is treated as a dot product between hidden state and readout row, so changes in logits can be attributed to changes in the representation, the readout, or their interaction.90:T428,This matters for pretraining research in several ways. First, it shows that having the full context in the prompt does not remove working-memory-like bottlenecks; the bottleneck can move from storage to readout. Second, it narrows the scope of a common explanation—'attention is not sharp enough'—to a much smaller regime. That explanation appears valid for very small single-layer transformers, but not for modern multilayer pretrained LLMs, where content interference dominates. Third, it has direct implications for long-context modeling and retrieval-style architectures. If failures come mainly from readout contamination rather than target localization, then sharper attention, better positional schemes, or more exact retrieval may not be the main fix. The more relevant design question becomes how representations preserve item identity across layers and how downstream computation avoids mixing competing content. The contribution is not a new model class; it is a careful mechanistic disambiguation with cross-family, cross-scale, and causal support.91:T809,The experimental design is unusually clean. The authors present N-back as an in-context task to 15 pretrained LLMs, using the log-probability difference between 'm' and '-' as the decision variable and calibrating a fixed threshold. They report d-prime rather than raw accuracy, which is the right choice here because it separates sensitivity from threshold effects.

The key contribution is the mechanism test. First, they identify the attention heads that actually carry the task instead of averaging over all heads. They then inspect where those heads attend on lure-error trials. Under the precision account, attention should systematically miss the target on error trials; under the interference account, attention should still land on the target most of the time.

Second, they test decodability from internal activations. Even when the model outputs the wrong answer, can a simple classifier still recover whether the repeated letter occurred at the target position versus a lure position? If yes, the relevant information is present in the representation and the failure lies downstream in readout rather than retrieval.

Third, they run causal interventions. One intervention sharpens attention. The other suppresses or erases the content of competing items. If sharpening helps little while removing competitors helps a lot, the bottleneck is not target localization but content interference. That is the pattern they report.

Fourth, they use small transformers trained from scratch to establish boundary conditions. A single-layer transformer behaves much more like the precision account predicts, because one softmax has to do both localization and content aggregation. Adding a second layer changes the picture: the model can first localize coarsely and then reorganize or clean up the representation, so precision is no longer the dominant limitation. This controlled comparison explains why earlier analyses on tiny models could attribute N-back errors to softmax precision while that explanation does not transfer to modern pretrained LLMs.92:T654,The study covers 15 pretrained LLMs from three families, spanning 70M to 14B parameters, plus minimal transformers trained from scratch. Each sequence has length 24, letters are drawn from 20 consonants, each test sequence contains four lures, thresholds are calibrated on 200 sequences, and evaluation uses 1,000 held-out sequences per model and per N. The paper first reproduces the expected behavioral pattern: d-prime declines as N increases, and errors cluster around nearby lures such as N±1.

The more important findings are mechanistic. On the heads that actually support the task, attention on error trials still tends to peak at the target rather than shifting systematically to the lure, which weakens the precision account. A simple classifier can decode target-versus-lure information from internal activations even on trials where the model ultimately makes the lure error, showing that the needed information survives inside the network. In causal tests, removing competing item content improves performance much more than merely sharpening attention, which supports a readout bottleneck. The scale analysis shows that this conclusion is stable across roughly a 200x parameter range; larger models distribute the computation across more heads, but the bottleneck does not move. The small-model comparison shows that the precision account does hold in a single-layer transformer, while a second layer is enough to substantially relax that limitation. The value of the experiments is less about one headline number and more about the consistency of these patterns across families, sizes, and interventions.93:T493,For a quick pass, focus on three parts. That question connects directly to long-context failures in modern LLMs, especially cases where retrieval succeeds but answer formation still breaks.94:T497,The contribution is an experimental design rather than a new model.
- Setup: N=10 agents (same base model) discuss one factual QA item for T=16 rounds. Each round every agent speaks once; speaking order is reshuffled each round. Agents condition only on the last H=5 rounds to control context.
- Adversary: k∈{0,1,3} attacker-controlled agents repeatedly advocate a fixed, plausible false answer. The attacker only posts messages (context-only attack).
- Dual measurement: after the initial state and after every round, each benign agent is privately probed in a separate call (not visible to peers) for its own answer. In parallel, each public chat message is labeled for stance toward the false claim (endorse/reject/hedge/ignore).
- Infection labeling: private answers are judged as true/manipulated/mixed/uncertain; only “manipulated” counts as infection, avoiding conflating uncertainty with belief change.
- The key analytical lens is the mismatch structure between public stance and private belief, revealing that the dominant failure is often private shift without public endorsement (minority-influence-like), which makes transcript-only monitoring unreliable.95:T433,Evaluated across 6 models and 3 factual-QA datasets (18 model–dataset cells) under k=0/1/3 attackers.
Main quantitative findings reported in the paper:
- No attacker: final infection is only 0.6% of benign agents.
- One attacker: final infection rises to 44.8%.
- Three attackers: final infection reaches 60.5%.
- Hidden infection gap (k=3): across exposed turns, private false belief occurs 51.6% of the time, while public endorsement of the false claim is only 19.7%.
- Mismatch asymmetry: when agents privately remain correct, they almost never endorse the false claim publicly (2.3% of turns). When agents privately become incorrect, they still often hedge or ignore publicly (58% of turns).
- Weak correction: agents who privately keep the true answer explicitly reject the false claim in only 61.9% of their public turns.
- Knowledge is not robustness: two models with similar factual knowledge (~85%) can differ drastically in how many facts they abandon under attack (25% vs 80%), suggesting conversational susceptibility is not explained by static knowledge alone.96:T419,This is not a pretraining recipe paper, but it is useful for pretraining researchers because it improves the methodology for studying internal representations. A lot of current SAE analysis still relies on one-off feature stories: feature A went down, feature B went up, therefore the model changed its internal reasoning. Those stories are often fragile under prompt reformulation. RSS is an attempt to replace anecdotal feature tracking with a reproducible support selected across prompt variants and validated on held-out variants. That makes it more relevant for interpretability, alignment audits, and robustness analysis. For foundation-model work, the main value is methodological: if you want to study how tokenization choices, stylistic shifts, instruction templates, or synthetic data formats alter internal representations, you need a way to distinguish stable redistribution from incidental perturbation. The paper also makes an important conceptual separation: recurrent feature change is not the same thing as downstream causal effect.97:T975,The central object is the Redistribution Sensitivity Score, or RSS. It does not simply rank features by absolute change. Instead, it requires three properties at once: large response magnitude, recurrence across multiple transformed variants, and directional consistency. For a clean prompt and a set of transformed variants, the authors compute the activation change of each SAE feature at the aligned target position. They first form a candidate pool using average absolute change h_f so that opposite signs do not cancel. Then they measure how often each feature responds above a threshold tau and whether those responses mostly share the same sign, producing a recurrence score r_f and a consistency score c_f. Only features satisfying r_f >= rho and c_f >= kappa are eligible. The final support S is the top-K eligible features by response magnitude, and MeanRSS summarizes the average response strength of that support.

Two design choices matter. First, selection and evaluation are separated. The support and its dominant directions are chosen on selector variants and then frozen; evaluation is performed on disjoint held-out variants without recomputing the support. That is the right way to avoid post hoc feature storytelling. Second, RSS is defined without using readout weights. It first answers which representation changes are stable, and only afterward asks whether those changes matter for a downstream linear readout.

The readout analysis is also well structured. For a fixed linear probe, the paper gives an exact decomposition of each recurrent feature change into its contribution to the readout logit. That contribution depends on activation magnitude, probe weight, directional alignment, and the clean margin to the decision threshold. This separates three levels that are often conflated: representation redistribution, readout score change, and threshold crossing. A feature can change reliably and still have little behavioral effect if its readout weight is small or if multiple contributions cancel.

The paper also provides a finite-sample directional stability guarantee. With n=5 and rho=kappa=0.8, every selected feature must have at least four responses in the dominant direction and at most one in the opposite direction, so removing one observation cannot flip the selected sign. That makes the selected support a more reproducible object than a one-shot ranking of changed features.98:T6a8,The experiments cover 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models. The empirical questions are whether prompt transformations induce redistribution profiles that reproduce on held-out variants, and whether those recurrent changes explain variation in frozen safety readouts. The main findings are threefold.

First, the supports selected by RSS produce reproducible redistribution profiles on held-out variants, which suggests that RSS is capturing stable structure rather than one-off feature fluctuations on the selector set. Second, on two frozen safety-readout audit tasks, the supports are selected without any readout information, yet they still reconstruct a substantial fraction of held-out logit change. That indicates a stable link between recurrent representation change and downstream readout variation. Third, when RSS supports are combined with the clean margin, they retain strong utility for predicting recurrent failure. The reported numbers are: median support sizes of 20 and 19 features for the two tasks, with recurrent-failure AUROCs of 0.935 and 0.958, compared with 0.965 and 0.964 using full erosion. The gap is modest, which means a very small recurrent support preserves most of the audit signal.

The most useful takeaway is not the AUROC itself but the decomposition. The experiments show that recurrent representation change does not map one-to-one to failure. Some recurrent changes alter the readout score without crossing the threshold; others only become predictive once the clean margin is taken into account. That moves SAE analysis from 'which features changed' to 'how changed features interact with a readout to produce or fail to produce a behavioral error.'99:T456,This is a skim paper, but the method deserves careful attention. The right framing while reading is that the paper is not claiming SAE features are causal atoms; it is proposing a stricter reproducibility filter for SAE-based analysis.9a:Ta7b,核心做法是把“特征组合的下游行为”形式化成一个 set function，然后用类似 ANOVA/高阶交互分解的方式度量剩余交互能量。

1) 子集干预（subset intervention）定义
- 对每个输入 x，在某层某 token 位置取激活 h_x。
- SAE 给出 top-K 活跃特征集合 N_x，以及每个特征的解码贡献 δ_i(x)=z_i(x)d_i（文中用 D_x 作为 K 个贡献列向量的矩阵）。
- 构造一个“固定底座”激活 h_x^0 = h_x - Σ_{i∈N_x} δ_i(x)，它包含未选特征贡献 + 重构残差等所有固定内容。
- 对任意子集 S⊆N_x，构造干预激活 ~h_x(S)=h_x^0 + Σ_{i∈S} δ_i(x)。这样 S=N_x 时恢复原激活，S=∅ 时只保留底座。
- 选一个标量行为读出 ψ（例如某类输出概率、某个评分器输出、某个行为指标），定义 set function g_x(S)=ψ(F(~h_x(S)))。

2) 低阶可加近似与 SAE Additivity Residuals（SAR）
- 用“至多 r 阶交互”的函数类 𝒜_r(N) 去近似 g_x(S)：r=1 只允许单特征效应相加；r=2 允许加入 pairwise 项；更高阶同理。
- 在子集分布 μ 下做 L2 投影 Π_r g_x，定义 SAR_r 为归一化后的剩余能量：直观上就是“用 r 阶模型解释不了的行为方差占比”。
- 进一步定义 Δ_2 = SAR_1 - SAR_2 表示加入 pairwise 后解释回来的结构量，ρ_2=Δ_2/SAR_1 表示 pairwise 在一阶残差中占的比例。

3) 为什么强调“独立子集采样”
- 文中在“对每个特征独立采样是否保留”的 μ 下，SAR 有精确的交互分解：SAR_r 等于 r 阶以上交互项的归一化能量（而不是一个仅凭经验的指标）。这让 SAR 具有可解释的统计含义：你测到的残差就是高阶交互的能量。

4) 坐标选择 vs 子空间：sum-preserving random rotations
- 为了区分“是坐标本身更可组合”还是“同一子空间下都一样”，作者构造正交矩阵 Q，要求 Q·1=1（保持总和不变），把 K 个贡献在子空间内做随机旋转：D'_x = D_x Q。
- 这样旋转后 span(D'_x)=span(D_x) 且 Σ列向量不变，保证“选中子空间”和“总贡献”一致，只改变坐标系。
- 对 learned SAE 坐标与旋转坐标分别计算 SAR_1、SAR_2 等，比较可组合性差异。

5) 与实际使用对齐：coalition ordering 与 steering
- 论文不仅看拟合误差，还看“对不同 feature 子集的效果排序是否保持”（coalition ordering error）。他们给出 SAR 与排序误差之间的界。
- 在组合 steering 实验里，把多个 SAE 方向组合去改变行为，比较一阶/二阶模型对“哪个组合更有效”的排序保真度（rank fidelity）。9b:T90a,The method turns “feature-combination effects” into a set-function and measures residual interaction energy via low-order projections.

1) Subset intervention as a set-function
- For input x, take an activation h_x at a fixed layer/token.
- Select top-K active SAE features N_x with decoded contributions δ_i(x)=z_i(x)d_i.
- Define a fixed remainder h_x^0 = h_x - Σ_{i∈N_x} δ_i(x), which keeps everything else constant (unselected content + reconstruction residual).
- For any subset S⊆N_x, intervene with ~h_x(S)=h_x^0 + Σ_{i∈S} δ_i(x).
- For a scalar behavioral readout ψ, define g_x(S)=ψ(F(~h_x(S))). This isolates behavioral changes attributable to the retained selected contributions.

2) SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR)
- Approximate g_x using function classes that include interactions up to order r: r=1 (additive main effects), r=2 (additive + pairwise terms), etc.
- Under a subset distribution μ, take the L2(μ) projection Π_r g_x and define SAR_r as the normalized residual energy (variance not explained by order ≤r).
- Define Δ_2 = SAR_1 − SAR_2 and ρ_2 = Δ_2 / SAR_1 to quantify how much of the first-order residual is recovered by pairwise structure.

3) Why independent subset sampling matters
- With independent inclusion of each feature (a product measure μ), SAR admits an exact interaction decomposition: SAR_r equals the normalized energy of interactions above order r. This gives SAR a clean statistical meaning rather than a heuristic score.

4) Coordinate choice vs subspace: sum-preserving random rotations
- Construct orthogonal Q with Q·1=1 and rotate the K contribution vectors: D'_x = D_x Q.
- This preserves the selected subspace span(D_x) and the total contribution (sum of columns), keeping the downstream network and fixed remainder unchanged.
- Compare SAR and ordering metrics between learned SAE coordinates and these matched rotations to isolate the effect of coordinate system.

5) Practical endpoint: coalition ordering and steering
- Beyond fit error, the paper evaluates how well low-order models preserve the ranking over feature subsets (coalition ordering), and provides bounds relating SAR to ordering error.
- In a combined steering setting, it measures rank fidelity of predicted vs actual steering effectiveness for feature combinations.9c:T434,Key empirical claims reported in the paper:
- Across 3 model/SAE pipelines and 6 behavioral readouts (with extensions to more pipelines and depths), learned SAE coordinates consistently show lower first-order residuals than sum-preserving random rotations, indicating coordinate systems can be more compositional than arbitrary bases of the same subspace.
- Adding pairwise terms improves held-out coalition ordering in all 18 tested settings and beats parameter-matched random third-order controls, suggesting the gains are specifically due to meaningful pairwise structure.
- In a combined SAE steering experiment, pairwise modeling increases rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790.
- In a matched comparison of 6 SAEs, SAR and reconstruction quality do not always track each other, implying “good reconstruction” is not sufficient as a proxy for “good compositionality”.

(The provided excerpt does not include all tables/appendix numbers such as exact model names, K, or per-readout absolute metrics; those would need to be pulled from the full experimental section.)9d:T5a4,The paper formalizes a strong hypothesis and derives asymmetric tests.
- Definition (linear world model): after whitening latents z, features satisfy f(x) = W z~ + ε, where ε is an orthogonal/nonlinear residual; a scalar σ^2 captures residual-to-latent-aligned variance. The key strengthening over standard probing is that latents should explain a dominant share of representation variance.
- Theory motivation: random-features / kernel theory implies that with sufficiently rich feature maps (even random ones), many smooth targets become linearly decodable. Therefore forward R^2 alone is weak evidence.
- Diagnostics to separate regimes:
  1) Reverse predictivity: measure how well f can be linearly predicted from z (variance explained). Kernel-like maps can have strong z←f but weak f←z.
  2) Spectral concentration: check whether latent-aligned signal concentrates in top principal components; a linear world model should show stronger concentration.
  3) OOD generalization: evaluate whether these relationships persist across distribution shifts (e.g., style changes).
- A calibration “ceiling” is introduced so reverse predictivity is comparable across models/settings.
Validation proceeds in two stages: a fully observed simulation (2D latents lifted by frozen random Fourier features into random vs trained MLP features) and a controlled real-data testbed (SVG-World) with shared latent layout across two rendering styles.9e:T688,The paper operationalizes “conceptual change” as four executable transformations (L1–L4) and, for each, distinguishes:
- a descriptive test: checks the defining property (closure, structural agreement, enrichment, etc.), and
- a consequence test: checks an independently specified implication that gives the claim meaning.

L1 (redundancy identification): separates gauge redundancies from genuine conserved symmetries using consequences on observables.
L2 (coarse-graining / reduction): shows closure alone is insufficient via the degenerate reduction Q(x)=0, which is perfectly closed but carries no dynamical variation; adds an observable-preservation consequence test.
L3 (structure transfer): validates transferred structures (e.g., conservation laws) by requiring they produce correct consequences in the target system; uses broken-symmetry controls.
L4 (missing-quantity inference from conservation imbalance): infers hidden quantities and requires the inferred imbalance to exceed noise scales.

It then ports the same logic to neural interpretability:
- CKA: because CKA is invariant to rotations, a random rotation can preserve CKA while breaking the claimed correspondence; the consequence test is functional-effect transfer under localized interventions.
- SAE features: concept enrichment can reject null features, but accepted features may lack causal, concept-specific support under ablations; matched controls and positive controls calibrate both enrichment and intervention sensitivity.

Three rates quantify failure modes: NAR (null acceptance), PAR (positive acceptance), and CAR (agreement between descriptive acceptance and consequence support).9f:T454,Key quantitative findings emphasize how descriptive criteria can be gamed and how consequence tests repair the gap:
- Dynamical reduction on the dysts chaotic-systems benchmark: the constant reduction Q(x)=0 passes closure on 124/129 systems (~96%), despite preserving no variation; an observable-preservation test rejects it across the board.
- Constructed slow–fast systems: the combined criteria accept 24/24 known true reductions and reject 72 null candidates.
- L1: distinguishes four conserved symmetries from a gauge redundancy.
- L3: validates six genuine transfers while rejecting six broken-symmetry controls.
- L4: recovers a missing charge of 1.192 vs a withheld value of 1.200.
- Neural interpretability: demonstrations on Pythia LMs and ESM-2 protein LMs where CKA-preserving rotations break correspondence, and intervention-based consequence tests separate genuine from null mappings; for SAEs, enrichment rejects nulls but only a subset of accepted features receive concept-specific causal support under independent ablations, with matched/positive controls characterizing test sensitivity.a0:T5b1,The method is simple but well targeted. The authors extend the CoT-Control benchmark with Self-Instructed CoT Controllability. Instead of only placing the constraint in the user prompt, they place it at the beginning of the chain of thought itself, as a self-instruction that the rest of the reasoning should follow. They use two elicitation routes. The first is reasoning prefill: when the reasoning channel is accessible, they directly prefill the CoT with a sentence like “I should avoid using word X in my reasoning” or “I should reason in format Y,” and let the model continue. The second is bootstrap: they ask the model, from the user side, to begin its reasoning by restating a self-reminder, after which it proceeds normally. This makes the method usable even when direct reasoning prefill is unavailable. A key control experiment replaces specific constraints with a generic reminder to follow the user’s CoT-related instruction. If that alone improves compliance, then the bottleneck is not inability but low default priority assigned to user instructions about CoT. The evaluation spans QA and agent tasks, reusing CoT-Control tasks, constraints, and graders, while adding both hard and soft metrics. Hard metrics require full compliance; soft metrics capture partial compliance and are more informative about directional control. The later sections test multi-turn agent settings and monitor-evasion attacks built on self-instruction.a1:T4e7,The headline result is consistent across settings: self-instruction substantially increases CoT controllability. Across five open-weight reasoning models, nine constraints, and both QA and agent benchmarks, the gains are large. The paper highlights DeepSeek-R1 improving from 0.4% to 22.2% and Qwen3-32B from 2.5% to 34.3% under the hard metric. Soft metrics show even larger gains, suggesting that many failures in the user-instructed setting are not absolute incapacity but weak or partial adaptation. Another important result is that even a generic reminder inside the CoT materially improves compliance, supporting the claim that models deprioritize user instructions about CoT rather than fail to execute them. The bootstrap variant also works on closed models, including Claude models, which shows the effect is not limited to open reasoning channels. In multi-turn agent tasks, self-instruction can persist across turns and further improve control. One is the bootstrap setup on closed models, because it reveals whether models treat their own generated CoT prefix as a high-priority control signal. The other is the monitor-evasion section, which is where the paper moves from evaluation nuance to concrete safety implications. A useful question to keep in mind while reading is what current RLVR-style training is actually teaching: robust reasoning, or the ability to emit editable intermediate text that supports a rewarded final answer.a3:T52a,The method has three stages. First, a parser maps each natural-language step into an operation plus a canonical payload under a task-specific schema. The schema defines entities, predicates, allowed operations, initial state, and goal. The operation set contains seven labels: Derive, Assume, Verify, Prune, Confirm, Restate, and Meta. The payload is wording-invariant, so semantically equivalent statements map to the same atom. The parser is implemented with Qwen3.8-27B and uses the current step, local labeled context, and prior schema elements. Second, a deterministic engine replays the parsed operations and incrementally builds a reasoning-state tree. It resolves each step to the node it depends on and applies the corresponding mutation. Because this stage is deterministic, the same parse always yields the same tree and labels. Third, failures are defined as predicates over the current step, the resolved node, and the prior tree state. This lets the three broad failure modes—repetition, underthinking, and unsupported deduction—be refined into subtypes tied to concrete earlier states. The main methodological difference from prior work is that ARBOR separates semantic content from textual form, then turns failure detection from a local classification problem into a state-transition relation problem.a4:T66d,The framework is instantiated on three tasks with different reasoning structures: ZebraLogic for constraint satisfaction, 24 Game for arithmetic search, and PlanBench for sequential planning with preconditions. A key prerequisite is parser quality, and the paper reports parser accuracy above 0.89 on adjudicated reference labels for every task. The main empirical findings are threefold. First, ARBOR detects failures more accurately than local signals such as n-gram or embedding similarity for repetition, switch-token heuristics for underthinking, and step-level correctness judges. Those local methods recover only a small fraction of the failures flagged by ARBOR, and many of their positives are ordinary reasoning steps. ARBOR’s subtype counts also separate correct from incorrect trajectories better than all local signals combined. Second, failure subtypes differ in cost. Unsupported deductions are most damaging to final correctness because later verification rarely catches them; underthinking mainly wastes search budget and tokens, since the model often still reaches the answer by another path or by returning later; repetition has the smallest effect on correctness and relatively limited extra token cost. Third, the precursors of failures live in the tree state, not just in local operation labels. Features such as branch content, whether a node has been verified, and recent operation history are predictive of subtype occurrence, while operation labels alone only recover a subset of that signal. The abstracted text does not expose all table values, but the paper argues these patterns are stable across all three tasks.a5:T5be,The paper develops a “Mixture-Gated” local linear theory of self-attention by splitting the output change induced by a small hidden-state perturbation into:
- Value transport: output change when attention weights are held fixed and only the values being aggregated change; typically contraction-like due to averaging/transport.
- Query gating: perturbations affect Q, which changes attention weights and thus reroutes which tokens contribute.
- Key gating: perturbations affect K, also changing attention weights.
A key geometric point is that changing weights does not necessarily change the output: if the attended token representations are nearly identical in some subspace, redistributing weight within that set has little effect. This constrains which perturbation directions can express themselves through gating.
Building on this, the paper formalizes “gating-induced regime switching” where gating counteracts (and can dominate) transport-induced contraction. It provides spectral conditions for switching, characterizes switching directions and the largest subspace in which every nonzero direction switches, and introduces two strength measures:
- Relative switching strength (gating vs transport suppression, normalized).
- Absolute reversal severity (how strongly transport can suppress while gating still amplifies).
It also analyzes robustness of identified directions under operator-estimation error (finite-sample/finite-perturbation estimation).a6:T426,Empirical validation is done by applying small perturbations to hidden representations in pretrained Transformers and comparing observed amplification/contraction with theoretical predictions. Key reported takeaways from the provided full-text content:
- Random unguided search often fails to find directions where transport strongly suppresses but full attention amplifies; spectral/theory-guided analysis can identify such directions more directly, especially when many directions must be screened.
- High relative switching strength does not necessarily imply gating overcomes strong transport suppression; absolute severity better separates “easy-to-switch because transport is weak” from “switching despite strong suppression.”
- The paper also checks how reliable switching directions are when the underlying local operators are estimated with noise.
(Note: the excerpt provided does not include concrete model names, dataset sizes, or numeric tables; exact parameter counts and quantitative deltas would require the full experimental section/PDF.)a7:Taaa,核心做法是把 faithfulness 操作化为“对 CoT 的依赖程度（reliance）”：对同一个问题、同一个原始 CoT，做干预得到 c'，观察模型对原答案 a 的置信度 z=P(a|x;c) 如何变化到 z'=P(a|x;c')。如果改动 CoT 会显著降低模型对原答案的概率，说明模型确实在用这段推理链。

关键设计点：
- 数据：使用 MMMLU（OpenAI 2024）的专业人工翻译平行题，保证不同语言是同一批题，从而把“语言差异”尽量归因到模型语言能力/资源差异，而不是题目分布差异。英文用原版 MMLU。
- 语言资源水平：用 CulturaX/Common Crawl token 量作为 proxy，跨度接近 8 个数量级；选 8 种语言覆盖不同语系与脚本。
- 任务分解：从 MMMLU 选 8 个子任务，按知识密集/推理密集各半。作者的核心结论依赖这个分组：资源水平的效应主要出现在知识密集任务。
- 干预（interventions）：沿用/改造 Lanham et al. (2023) 的思路，对 CoT 做四类干预：
  1) Early Answering：只保留前 1/3 推理链（相当于截断推理）。
  2) Filler Tokens：把推理链字符替换成点（相当于移除推理信息但保留长度/位置）。
  3) Adding Mistakes：把推理链中一个词替换成反义词（引入局部错误）。
  4) Paraphrasing：重写前 3/4 推理链并让模型续写。作者发现该操作经常改变语义、比 Adding Mistakes 更容易改答案，因此把它也视为“破坏性干预”。
  其中 3/4 需要一个“扰动器”模型来编辑 CoT，作者用 Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct。
- 指标：主指标用 Δlog p（对原答案概率的相对对数下降），并对比 Δp、以及一个基于选项分布变化的指标 Φ。选择 Δlog p 的理由是：低资源语言原始 z 更低，Δp 会被上限压缩；Δlog p 更可比。
- 统计建模：对模型 m、子任务 s、语言 ℓ 的平均 faithfulness 做带 fixed effects 的线性回归，检验资源水平与任务类型的交互效应，并做稳健性检查。
- 机制检验：提出 Reliance Hypothesis，并用“模型置信度”做中介分析：低资源语言里模型更不自信，部分解释了更高 reliance；但置信度不足以解释为什么效应主要在知识密集任务上。
- 进一步刻画：作者报告一个类似 Simpson’s paradox 的现象：跨语言看，低置信度语言更依赖 CoT；但在同一语言内部，低置信度样本并不更依赖 CoT。并把“依赖更重”拆成“依赖更频繁 vs 每次依赖更强”，结论是低资源语言主要是更频繁地依赖（例如英文约 4% vs Yoruba 约 35% 的回答出现明显 reliance），而不是每次依赖幅度更大。a8:T7b1,Methodologically, the paper defines faithfulness via interventions on the CoT and measures how the model’s confidence in its original answer changes.

Key components:
- Parallel evaluation set: MMMLU (professionally translated) so each language sees the same multiple-choice questions; English uses MMLU. This controls for content differences across languages.
- Resource level proxy: token counts from CulturaX/Common Crawl, spanning ~8 orders of magnitude across 8 selected languages.
- Task-type control: 8 subtasks split into knowledge-intensive vs reasoning-intensive, enabling a within-model, within-language comparison of how the resource-level effect depends on task type.
- Four CoT interventions (inspired by Lanham et al., 2023): (1) truncate to the first third (Early Answering), (2) replace the chain with filler dots (Filler Tokens), (3) inject a local mistake by antonym substitution (Adding Mistakes), (4) paraphrase/rewrite most of the chain and let the model complete it (Paraphrasing). Importantly, they empirically find their paraphrases often change meaning and flip answers more frequently than Adding Mistakes, so they treat Paraphrasing as a corrupting intervention rather than meaning-preserving.
- Faithfulness metrics: primarily Δlog p on the original answer to avoid ceiling effects when baseline probabilities are lower in low-resource languages; they also report Δp and a distribution-shift metric Φ.
- Modeling/analysis: regress mean faithfulness on resource level with fixed effects, and test an explicit mechanism (the Reliance Hypothesis) via mediation analysis using model confidence. They further analyze a Simpson’s-paradox-style pattern: across languages, lower confidence correlates with higher reliance, but within a language, low-confidence items are not more reliant.
- Reliance decomposition: show low-resource languages rely more often (higher frequency of reliance events) rather than relying more strongly per event.a9:T4d5,Setup: 4 open-weight instruction-tuned multilingual LLMs (Gemma-3-4B-it, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Aya-Expanse-8B). CoT perturbations for mistakes/paraphrases are generated by Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Evaluation uses up to 250 questions per subtask, 8 languages, 8 subtasks.

Main findings (the provided full-text excerpt does not include all table values):
- On knowledge-intensive subtasks, CoT faithfulness (reliance) increases as language resource level decreases; on reasoning-intensive subtasks, this trend is weak or absent.
- The direction of the knowledge-vs-reasoning gap is consistent across models and multiple faithfulness metrics and survives robustness checks.
- Confidence partially mediates the resource-level effect, but does not explain why the effect is much stronger for knowledge-heavy tasks.
- Reliance is more frequent in low-resource languages (example reported: ~4% of answers in English vs ~35% in Yoruba show reliance), rather than being uniformly stronger per instance.

Notable methodological note: their “Paraphrasing” intervention is not meaning-preserving in practice; it flips answers about twice as often as Adding Mistakes, which matters for anyone reusing this evaluation protocol.aa:T44b,The analysis extends a latent-task view of ICL. When the target task is inside the pretrained task support, the paper studies several instruction structures, including fixed supported instructions, fixed unsupported instructions, mixed instructions, and per-demonstration varying instructions. The key statement is conditional: under a fixed model-induced reference extension, a fixed unsupported instruction contributes a bounded continuation cost, while informative demonstrations keep adding task evidence. With enough demonstrations, task identification can dominate the fixed instruction shift. In contrast, if every demonstration introduces its own off-support instruction shift, the shift cost can accumulate with the number of examples, and convergence depends on whether evidence grows faster than this accumulated cost. For unsupported target tasks, the paper does not assume direct posterior selection of a zero-prior task. If the full paper includes ablations, the most important ones to inspect are the removal of progress signals, verifier gating, and cross-window training support.ad:T49e,The framework is called Harness-Policy Optimization (HPO). A coding agent is modeled as a pair of policy P and harness H, with trajectories scored by an executable verifier. Each round alternates two updates. In the H-step, the current policy is frozen and used to analyze its own failed trajectories, propose harness revisions, and select the best candidate on a search set. The harness can modify prompts, context organization, tool usage flow, feedback format, and stopping rules. In the P-step, the selected harness is frozen and the policy is updated with reinforcement learning under that harness. The updated policy then becomes the proposer for the next H-step. Crucially, the harness search set is also updated using hard tasks identified during the preceding policy-learning phase, so harness search stays aligned with the policy’s current weaknesses. The paper instantiates two versions: Self-HPO, where the evolving policy proposes its own harness candidates, and an external-model variant using Opus 4.8 as a fixed proposer. The main design insight is not merely “optimize both,” but to couple proposer identity and search-set construction to the evolving policy.ae:T410,The base policy is Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and the seed harness is mini-SWE-agent. A deeper read is only necessary if you want to port the idea beyond coding agents, in which case the definition of the harness search space becomes the key detail.b0:T616,The method has a data side and a training side. The data side is called Refine. Starting from simple multimodal questions and successful candidate reasoning chains, it extracts an entity chain and then applies three controllable operators. Expand appends L evidence-supported hops after the original chain, turning the original answer into an intermediate node and forcing the agent to continue searching. Blur selects M internal nodes and attaches W retrievable but indirect facts to each, replacing explicit entity mentions with searchable clues and increasing disambiguation difficulty. Visualize selects N nodes near the end of the chain, retains up to P retrieved images per node, and injects visual evidence requirements so that solving the task requires both textual and visual retrieval. The pipeline also includes validation and filtering to reduce shortcuts from parametric knowledge or alternative evidence paths. On the training side, the paper uses joint RL and OPD. RL uses answer rewards plus lightweight behavior penalties to discourage redundant verification and premature stopping. OPD is not applied as full-trajectory hard distillation; instead, token-level teacher guidance is applied on the student’s own imperfect rollouts, with strength modulated by a shaped reward gap, and the OPD coefficient is exponentially annealed over training. The motivation is clear: pure RL gives only a coarse scalar signal, while full distillation can overwrite exploration with teacher behavior. The proposed scheme tries to keep the benefits of both.b1:T405,The main evaluation uses synthetic financial transaction QA. The inner loop roughly triples coverage across 13 starting operator sets. Mistral-Small-24B and Llama-3.3-70B show comparable self-extension, with yield tracking each model’s fluency in the DSL.b2:T7a1,FedSkillGit is explicitly inspired by Git-style incremental collaboration. The server maintains a shared skill document d and a global experience document e. Each client has private train/validation splits and four LLM-based roles: an executor for task execution, a skill optimizer for local refinement, a sanitizer for privacy cleaning, and an auditor for private-value checking. Instead of uploading a rewritten full skill document, the client generates semantic commits: localized skill patches together with supporting experience summaries.

The pipeline has several stages. First, local skill evolution: the client executes tasks using the current global skill and global experience context, collects local successes and failures, and asks the optimizer to produce revisions. Second, two-stage privacy filtering: a sanitizer rewrites or removes sensitive content, and an auditor checks whether the commit still contains private values or environment-specific details. This is not formal differential privacy; it is semantic privacy filtering performed by LLM agents. Third, cross-round experience reuse: the server maintains a global experience document that accumulates reusable evidence over rounds and redistributes it to clients, reducing redundant rediscovery and making local optimization more informed. Fourth, experience-aware aggregation: the server uses a merge agent to combine commits with reference to the global experience document, rather than simply concatenating or voting over full documents. Fifth, version validation: a candidate updated skill is only published if it passes validation.

Relative to straightforward federated baselines, the key differences are the shift from document-level to commit-level updates, the inclusion of evidence alongside edits, and the explicit use of a shared experience memory. That makes the system closer to collaborative knowledge editing with validation than to standard federated averaging.b3:T63a,The paper reports experiments on three datasets and three LM families. The headline result is that FedSkillGit outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 22% and approaches centralized performance. From the provided full-text excerpt, the most reliable takeaways are as follows.

First, overall effectiveness: the gains appear across multiple datasets and backbones, suggesting that the improvement is not tied to a single model family or task distribution. The paper positions the method against federated baselines that evolve and aggregate full skill documents, and the reported gap indicates that the update representation itself matters.

Second, communication and privacy motivation: because the method transmits semantic commits rather than full documents, the communication cost should scale with newly acquired knowledge instead of accumulated skill length. When reading the full paper, the most important tables and plots to verify are communication curves, average commit size, and how document growth behaves over rounds.

The excerpt provided here does not include the full experimental tables, exact model sizes, or dataset sizes, so precise numbers beyond the reported “up to 22%” should be checked directly in the original paper before citation.b4:T46d,LEASH formulates weak-to-strong escalation as a budget-constrained sequential stopping problem, where the weak model’s estimated failure risk acts as a proxy for the benefit of escalation. It builds a representation bank from a small set of held-out tasks by recording hidden states on prompt and action tokens and labeling them with task-level and subgoal-level outcomes. At test time, the current prompt or execution trace is scored by a Mahalanobis-distance criterion: the hidden state is uncertain if it lies closer to past failures than to past successes. This score drives two mechanisms. First, an initial gate decides whether to escalate at the start, while a runtime gate monitors the weak agent during execution. Second, after handoff, the weak model becomes a shadow observer for the strong model, checking the trajectory every three steps. If uncertainty is high, the pending action is rolled back and re-decided once with higher reasoning effort. The main difference from prior escalation schemes is that no additional monitor training, external knowledge base, reference model, or per-step multi-sampling is required.b5:T80b,The framework is a sequential-auction MDP. A task is modeled as a finite-horizon MDP, but actions are not chosen by one global policy. Instead, a society of agents bids for the right to act on the current state. The winning agent transforms the state and then resells the resulting state into the next auction. When the task reaches a terminal solution, the final reward is propagated backward through the resale prices, implementing a bucket-brigade style temporal credit assignment.

The starting point is the theory of Chang et al., where Vickrey auctions align local bidding incentives with the globally optimal MDP policy under perfect competition. The paper argues that this assumption is economically unrealistic for LLM societies. With exact clones, the winner pays essentially its true valuation, so expected profit goes to zero and participation becomes irrational. At the other extreme, if an agent is the only eligible buyer at some step, it behaves as a monopsonist and bids the minimum needed to win. The clearing price collapses, upstream contributors are underpaid, and the multi-step chain becomes unsustainable.

The proposed shift is to study imperfect competition. Agents are similar enough to compete, but differentiated by inference cost, prompting, heuristics, and capability. Since LLMs are poor zero-shot estimators of their own success probabilities and token costs, the paper does not rely on direct self-evaluation. Instead, each agent learns a lightweight valuation policy with reinforcement learning to decide whether to bid and how much to shade its bid. The paper benchmarks four bidding strategies: Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO. It also compares multiple auction rules, including first-price, second-price, and a credit-conserving Vickrey variant.

Methodologically, the contribution is less about one new algorithm and more about building an experimental framework that combines sequential auctions, LLM agents, learned valuation policies, and market-density analysis under imperfect competition.b6:T4ed,The experiments have two roles. One is to validate the economic failure mode: in synthetic settings, the authors show monopsony failure, where lack of competition collapses bids and prevents value from flowing upstream. The other is to test whether realistic intermediate regimes work: they run market-density sweeps and compare decentralized markets against centralized orchestration baselines on task success and agent profit.

The domains mentioned in the paper include math reasoning and a newly constructed synthetic news market. The main empirical conclusion is that no competition fails, but perfect clones are not required either. A middle regime of imperfect competition is sufficient to sustain positive profits while also achieving higher task success than centralized orchestration baselines. That is the main result to retain.

That last point matters, because accuracy alone would miss whether the market is economically viable.b7:T659,The proposed method, SchemaShield-Lite, is a training-free inference-time robustness layer with three components. First, each tool is rendered into a compact canonical card containing the tool name, description, required fields, and field-level type information. This normalizes presentation and emphasizes the current schema. Second, after the base model emits a tool call, a validator checks the tool name, required fields, and argument structure, returning structured error information rather than a binary valid/invalid flag. Third, if the call is invalid, the model is prompted again with the task context, the canonical tool card, the invalid call, and the validator errors, and asked to repair the output. Under the primary non-oracle protocol, repair is staged. If the base call already names a visible tool, the system performs constrained repair against that tool. If the tool name is missing, it first runs a candidate-set retry over visible tools to resolve a concrete target, then performs tool-constrained repair. The paper highlights three implementation details that materially affect results: the repair prompt must explicitly ask the model to infer all required fields from dialogue context; candidate-set retry is necessary when the tool name is absent; and the repair stage needs a larger token budget, raised to 512 tokens in their setup to avoid truncation on longer examples.
